title: Order of integration: I(0), I(1) — and why it matters

explain.prompt: In 4–6 sentences: what are the orders of integration of log Brent, log WTI and the log spread log(Brent) − log(WTI)? Why is it remarkable that the spread is I(0) while each price is I(1), and what does it suggest economically? Why must both prices be I(1) before testing for cointegration?
rubric: log Brent and log WTI are I(1): unit root in levels (ADF does not reject, KPSS rejects), stationary after one difference.
The log spread is I(0): a combination of two I(1) series that is stationary — the definition of cointegration (here with a coefficient fixed at 1).
Economically: the WTI discount fluctuates around a stable value (≈ 6 %) and returns to it — the arbitrage of 2.1 at work; the two prices share one stochastic trend.
Cointegration is defined for series with the same order of integration (typically I(1)); with an I(0) series there is no common stochastic trend to share, and the test would be meaningless.
I(2) is rare in prices; if a series looks I(2), suspect a structural break first.
If the spread with coefficient 1 is already stationary, it can be studied directly without estimating β — but estimating β tests whether 1 is the right coefficient.
